sourceObjectiveEnglish: Personal a: Use personal a before a specific person who is a direct object: veo a Ana.
sourceSpeakingEnglish: Role-play Encontrar a los amigos with a patient classmate. Practice personal a. Use this lesson's grammar, ask a related question, answer the partner, and confirm understanding. Keep language at beginner level; explain unfamiliar words in English when asked.

cards.proposalNote: La is the feminine article “the” (la porte) or a direct-object pronoun meaning “her” or “it” before a verb (je la cherche).
Choose by context: dans means inside, sur means on top of, and à can name a place. These are separate words, not interchangeable.
Professeure is a female teacher; enseignante is another common term.
Use mon before a masculine singular noun (mon livre), ma before a feminine singular noun (ma sœur), and mon before a feminine noun starting with a vowel sound (mon amie).

cards.sourceSpanish: Busco a Ana en la biblioteca.
cards.sourceEnglish: I am looking for Ana in the library.
cards.proposedFrench: Je cherche Ana à la bibliothèque.
cards.proposalNote: À la bibliothèque can mean in or at the library.

cards.sourceSpanish: Veo a Luis cerca de la puerta.
cards.sourceEnglish: I see Luis near the door.
cards.proposedFrench: Je vois Luis près de la porte.

cards.sourceEnglish: We are visiting the teacher today.
cards.proposedFrench: Nous rendons visite à la professeure aujourd’hui.
cards.proposalNote: To visit a person, use rendre visite à. The à belongs to this verb construction.

candidateGrammar.explanation: In French, a noun that is the direct object of chercher (to look for), voir (to see), or connaître (to know) follows the verb directly, whether it is a person or a thing: je cherche Ana, je vois Luis, je connais ma sœur, je cherche mon livre. Chercher already includes the English “for” in “look for”; say je cherche Ana, not je cherche pour Ana. Some verbs require à as part of their construction: to visit a person, say rendre visite à (nous rendons visite à la professeure). A direct-object pronoun goes before the verb: je la cherche (I am looking for her).

sourceConflict.personalA: The Spanish personal a before a specific human direct object has no parallel French marking rule. Proposed French chercher/voir/connaître take direct objects here; rendre visite à has verb-governed à. Qualified curriculum review must distinguish these.
sourceConflict.card3: French la can be the feminine article or object pronoun; this lesson has no source sentence using the object-pronoun sense.
sourceConflict.card4: French dans, sur and à are contextual location alternatives, not interchangeable answers for in/on/at.
sourceConflict.card7AndReader3: The Spanish source names a female teacher, while its English Reader says only teacher; the proposed French professeure selects female gender, so bilingual scoring and dictionary display need explicit review.
sourceConflict.card8: French mon and ma depend on possessed noun sound and gender, not the single grouped English my gloss.
sourceConflict.card9: The proposed à la bibliothèque can mean in or at the library, but the source English says in. Qualified review must select contextual acceptance.
